# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

response:
I've read it. This comment confirms most of what I raised about the Halden paper, so I've checked it with extra care against confirming my own earlier view. Sections 1–5 hold up well. The abstract and conclusion go further than the authors' own evidence allows.

## What it argues

Using Halden's microdata, Varga and Holm document four problems:

1. **Attrition.** Seven of the nine withdrawals happened *after* the schedule began, not in preparation. Six of the nine cited workload or output.
2. **Output measure.** In the 23 organisations with records, manager indices exceed record-based output by 3.8 points on average, and the manager's figure is higher in 19 of the 23.
3. **Hours.** In the 27 organisations with time tracking, actual hours fell 14.1%, not 20%.
4. **Revenue.** Deflated by 4.1% CPI, revenue fell about 2.6% in real terms.

In the 17 organisations with both records and time tracking, the per-hour gain drops from 23.4% to 10.8%. The sectoral claim is an artifact of the per-hour metric, and Varden's counter stratum is called the most reliable finding in the literature.

The comment then argues:

- The remaining 10.8% is novelty, based on the energy decay in Halden's survey.
- Varden's meetings hypothesis is a post-hoc fit and should not be cited.
- Reduced-hours per-hour gains are therefore "entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty".

The data note concedes that the corrected estimates describe non-random subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

## What holds

I checked the arithmetic:

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Record-based output, scheduled hours: 95.1/0.8 | +18.9% ✓ |
| Hours ratio 34.6/40.3 = 0.859; 98.4/0.859 | +14.6% ✓ |
| Hours ratio 34.8/40.4 = 0.861; 95.4/0.861 | +10.8% ✓ |
| Revenue: 1.014/1.041 | −2.6% ✓ |

Sections 1–5 are well supported.

**The attrition finding is the most consequential new fact.** If the microdata show seven withdrawals after the schedule started, the Halden paper's description ("withdrew during the preparation phase") is factually wrong, not merely a matter of interpretation. Measured from enrolment, continuation is 56 of 70, or 80%.

**The manager–record gap is systematic.** Nineteen of 23 in one direction is unlikely by chance; a sign test gives p ≈ 0.003. The authors also frame it fairly as optimism, not bad faith.

**The record-based retail figure is weak on its own.** It rests on only three organisations. It is credible because it agrees with Varden's randomised counter stratum.

## Errors and gaps in the corrections

**1. The abstract claims a correction the analysis doesn't make.**

It says "correcting the first three" problems gives 10.8%, and the first three include attrition. Table 2 corrects only the output measure and hours. Attrition is described but never quantified.

A rough bound shows it matters, but modestly. Suppose the nine withdrawers had an output index of 85. Then:

(61 × 98.7 + 9 × 85) / 70 ≈ 96.9

That is about 2 points off the index under a fairly pessimistic assumption. The microdata would allow a proper bounds analysis.

**2. The hours decomposition doesn't add up.**

Actual pilot hours are 34.6, which is 2.6 hours above the scheduled 32. The stated sources, 0.7 extra hours on each of four days plus 1.6 hours on the day off, sum to 4.4. One of these figures, or the baseline the "+0.7" is measured against, needs checking.

**3. The novelty extrapolation is miscalculated, and it measures the wrong thing.**

The calculation:

- Energy fell from 0.61 SD at month three to 0.29 SD at month six, a slope of about −0.107 SD per month.
- Extrapolated linearly from those two points, it reaches zero at about month 8.7, not "around month ten".

The bigger problem is that energy is not output. Halden collected the output index *monthly*, and Varga and Holm have the microdata. If novelty drives the gain, output per hour should decline from month one to month six. That is a direct test, sitting in the data they already hold, and it isn't run.

**4. Record-based output may be biased downward in professional services.**

One of the record types is billable hours delivered. That measures time worked, not output, so it falls almost automatically when hours fall. If professional services firms (19 of 61 organisations) supplied billable-hours records, the record-based index understates any real gain there. The comment should say which records came from which sectors.

## Where the conclusion overreaches

**1. "Entirely an artifact" is contradicted by the evidence the comment itself relies on.**

The authors call Varden the most reliable evidence, but cite only its counter stratum. Varden's case-processing stratum avoids every problem in sections 1–3:

- It is randomised, with no reported attrition.
- Output comes from administrative records.
- Hours come from timesheets.
- Control staff also knew a trial was under way.

It still found +12.5% output per actual hour, with a confidence interval of +6.9 to +18.4. That was at nine months, beyond the point where the authors' own extrapolation says enthusiasm should have returned to baseline.

That doesn't prove durability, since Varden's 24-month follow-up is what will settle it. It does mean the comment cites one stratum of a trial as the best evidence while setting aside the other stratum, which contradicts its thesis.

**2. The comment demands proof of durability but asserts its own claim without proof.**

It says "the burden of proof lies with those claiming [durability]", then states as its conclusion that the gain is *entirely* artifact. Its own analysis leaves a 10.8% gain that it attributes to novelty without testing that attribution.

The defensible position is that durability is open: not shown and not refuted. The monthly Halden output trajectory and Varden's 24-month follow-up are what would close it. This is the "closing early" failure, applied to a sceptical conclusion.

**3. The meetings section attacks a claim Varden didn't make.**

Varden called the analysis unregistered and exploratory, said explicitly that seven offices "cannot establish a mechanism", and registered a confirmatory test. "It should not be cited as a mechanism" is something Varden already says.

The comment also says the data were "selected for analysis after the results were known". In fact the data were collected in month six, at managers' request, before the nine-month results existed.

The hypothesis also matters for the comment's own argument. Removing meetings predicts a gain that *persists*, because meetings that have been cancelled stay cancelled. That is the direct alternative to novelty. As I worked out last time, if baselines were similar, meeting removal alone could account for most of Varden's case-processing gain.

Halden's interviews add independent support: 47 of 58 managers mentioned cutting meetings. Dismissing the hypothesis drops the explanation the comment most needs to rule out, at the stage where it is most testable.

**4. The conclusion generalises beyond what the data note allows.**

The data note says the estimates describe non-random subsets of one pilot. The conclusion then makes claims about "reduced-hours schemes" in general.

## A conclusion the evidence supports

> *"Halden's 23.4% gain is overstated: correcting output to records and hours to actual time reduces it to about 11% in the organisations where both are possible, and attrition likely reduces it further. Halden misreported when organisations withdrew. In coverage-bound work, reduced hours reduce output (consistent with Varden). Whether the remaining per-hour gain is durable is open: Varden's randomised case-processing stratum shows +12.5% at nine months, which novelty alone does not obviously explain, and Halden's monthly output data and Varden's 24-month follow-up can test it."*

On my own earlier notes: I guessed the true Halden figure would be about half the reported one, and 10.8% against 23.4% is about half. I also called continuation "real evidence". With 80% continuation from enrolment, and withdrawers concentrated among the organisations that struggled, it is weaker evidence than I credited.

I can write this up as a referee report on the comment. I can also sketch the two analyses the authors could run with the microdata they already hold: the monthly output trajectory and the attrition bounds.
